items.stem: Which sugar, when attached to the H antigen, gives a red cell its A specificity?
items.why: The A gene codes for a glycosyltransferase that adds **N-acetyl-D-galactosamine** to the terminal galactose of the H antigen. Without H (which needs L-fucose first), neither the A nor the B sugar can be attached.

whyNot.0: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine is part of the type 1/type 2 precursor chain backbone, not the A-specific sugar.
whyNot.1: L-fucose defines the H antigen; it is the required acceptor structure, not the A determinant.
whyNot.3: D-galactose is the immunodominant sugar of the B antigen, added by the B-gene transferase.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system chapter

items.stem: A patient's red cells are nonreactive with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H lectin (Ulex europaeus). Her serum strongly agglutinates A1 cells, B cells, and group O screening cells at room temperature and at 37 °C, and her autologous control is negative. These results are best explained by:
options: A2 subgroup with anti-A1 in the serum
Group O with a cold-reacting alloantibody
A cold autoantibody (anti-I) interfering with typing
items.why: Bombay individuals (hh) cannot make H antigen, so their red cells lack H, A and B and do not react with Ulex lectin. Their serum contains anti-A, anti-B and a potent anti-H that reacts over a wide thermal range, so **group O cells, which carry the most H antigen, are strongly agglutinated**.

whyNot.0: A2 cells agglutinate with anti-A reagent, and anti-A1 would not react with group O screening cells.
whyNot.1: Group O cells have the greatest amount of H antigen and would react strongly with anti-H lectin.
whyNot.2: An autoantibody would also react with the patient's own cells, making the autologous control positive.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system chapter (Bombay phenotype)

items.stem: A woman whose red cells type D-positive with routine anti-D reagent is found to have alloanti-D after delivering a D-positive infant. Investigation shows her red cells lack certain epitopes of the D antigen. Her phenotype is best described as:
options: Weak D caused by a reduced number of otherwise complete D sites
items.why: Partial D red cells lack one or more D epitopes, so the person can form alloanti-D against the missing epitopes after exposure to conventional D-positive cells. **The defining feature is a qualitative (missing epitope) change**, and such cells may still type D-positive with many reagents.

whyNot.1: Del cells carry so little D that it is detected only by adsorption-elution, so they would type D-negative routinely.
whyNot.2: Classic weak D reflects a quantitative reduction of D sites that carry essentially all epitopes; these individuals generally do not make alloanti-D.
whyNot.3: Rhnull cells lack all Rh antigens and would type D-negative.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter

items.stem: Seven days after transfusion, a patient has a falling hemoglobin, jaundice, and a newly positive DAT. The pretransfusion antibody screen was negative. The eluate contains an antibody known for showing dosage, binding complement, and dropping to undetectable levels in vivo. Which antibody is most likely?
items.why: Kidd antibodies are a classic cause of delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions: they are often weak, show dosage, can bind complement, and fall below detectable levels quickly. Re-exposure to the antigen then triggers an anamnestic response, producing **hemolysis several days after a transfusion that looked compatible**.

whyNot.1: Anti-P1 is typically a weak cold-reacting IgM antibody that is seldom clinically significant.
whyNot.2: Anti-M is usually a naturally occurring cold-reactive IgM antibody and is rarely clinically significant.
whyNot.3: Anti-Lea is usually a naturally occurring IgM antibody and rarely causes hemolytic transfusion reactions.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other blood group systems chapter (Kidd)

items.stem: Midway through a whole blood donation, a donor becomes pale and sweaty and says she feels faint. What should the phlebotomist do first?
options: Lower the collection bag further so the unit fills faster and can be completed
Release the tourniquet and remove the needle to stop the collection
Give the donor oral fluids while the collection continues
Have the donor stand up and walk to improve circulation
items.why: Pallor, sweating and faintness signal a vasovagal reaction. **The first step is to stop the donation** by releasing the tourniquet and withdrawing the needle; then the donor is positioned with legs raised, tight clothing loosened, a cold compress applied and vital signs monitored.

whyNot.0: Continuing the draw to finish the unit puts the donor at greater risk; the donor's safety comes before the unit.
whyNot.2: Fluids may help during recovery, but continuing the collection while the donor is symptomatic is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Standing up can worsen the drop in blood pressure and lead to a fall and injury.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Donor selection chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.), Allogeneic and autologous blood donor selection

items.stem: Adding adenine to CPD (to make CPDA-1) extends red cell storage from 21 to 35 days mainly because adenine:
options: Keeps 2,3-DPG at normal levels throughout storage
Acts as the main buffer against the fall in pH
Serves as a substrate for red cell ATP synthesis
items.why: Red cells use adenine to resynthesize ATP, and **maintaining ATP improves post-transfusion red cell viability**, which allows the longer shelf life. The other ingredients of the solution have separate roles: citrate anticoagulates, dextrose fuels glycolysis and phosphate buffers.

whyNot.0: 2,3-DPG falls steadily during storage in CPDA-1; adenine does not prevent this.
whyNot.1: Buffering is provided mainly by the phosphate in the solution, not adenine.
whyNot.2: Calcium chelation is the job of citrate, the anticoagulant in the solution.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual (current ed.), Blood component collection, processing and storage; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Red blood cell preservation chapter. Philippine DOH/NVBSP rules may specify their own requirements; follow local regulation in practice.

items.stem: Today, Cryoprecipitated AHF is most often transfused to:
options: Raise the platelet count in a thrombocytopenic patient
Replace fibrinogen in hypofibrinogenemia, such as in massive bleeding or DIC
Replace the vitamin K-dependent factors during warfarin reversal
items.why: Cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII and fibronectin. Because factor VIII deficiency and von Willebrand disease are now treated mainly with factor concentrates, **its main use is fibrinogen replacement**.

whyNot.0: Cryoprecipitate contains no meaningful platelets; thrombocytopenia is treated with platelet components.
whyNot.1: Factor IX is not concentrated in cryoprecipitate; it stays in the cryo-poor plasma, and hemophilia B is treated with factor IX concentrate.
whyNot.3: Factors II, VII, IX and X are not concentrated in cryoprecipitate; prothrombin complex concentrate or plasma is used.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Blood component preparation and therapy chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: A patient will receive red cells donated by his brother as a directed donation. Which modification of the unit is required to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD)?
items.why: A blood relative may be homozygous for an HLA haplotype the recipient shares, so the recipient's immune system does not reject the donor's T cells, which can then engraft and attack the host. Irradiation (at least 25 Gy to the center of the unit and at least 15 Gy elsewhere) **stops donor lymphocytes from proliferating** and is the accepted method of prevention.

whyNot.1: Leukoreduction lowers the number of white cells but does not reliably remove all viable lymphocytes, so it is not acceptable for preventing TA-GVHD.
whyNot.2: Washing removes plasma proteins but leaves enough viable lymphocytes to cause TA-GVHD.
whyNot.3: CMV-seronegative selection reduces the risk of CMV transmission, not TA-GVHD.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual (current ed.), Blood component modification (irradiation); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Blood component preparation and therapy chapter. Philippine DOH/NVBSP rules may specify their own requirements; follow local regulation in practice.

items.stem: About 2 hours into a plasma transfusion, a patient develops sudden respiratory distress, hypoxemia, fever, and hypotension. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates, there is no evidence of circulatory overload, and diuretics do not help. The donor is a multiparous woman with HLA class I antibodies. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.why: TRALI is acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that occurs within 6 hours of transfusion, often with fever and hypotension. Donor antibodies to HLA or neutrophil (HNA) antigens, most often from multiparous women, are the usual cause, and **the absence of volume overload separates it from TACO**.

whyNot.0: TACO usually shows hypertension, signs of volume overload such as raised BNP, and improvement with diuretics.
whyNot.1: Anaphylaxis begins within minutes with bronchospasm, urticaria and shock, without fever or new bilateral infiltrates.
whyNot.2: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction causes fever and chills but not hypoxemia or pulmonary infiltrates.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion reactions chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.), Noninfectious complications of transfusion

items.stem: A patient with anti-c and anti-Jka needs 2 crossmatch-compatible red cell units. In the donor population, 80% of units are c-positive and 77% are Jka-positive. Assuming the two antigens are inherited independently, what is the minimum number of ABO-compatible units that should be screened to expect 2 units that are negative for both antigens?
items.why: Multiply the antigen-NEGATIVE frequencies (1 - 0.80 = 0.20 and 1 - 0.77 = 0.23): 0.20 × 0.23 = 0.046, so 4.6% of donors lack both antigens. Divide the number of units needed by this frequency: 2 / 0.046 = 43.5, which is rounded up to **44 units**.

whyNot.0: 4 results from using the antigen-positive frequencies (0.80 × 0.77 = 0.616; 2 / 0.616 = 3.2) instead of the antigen-negative ones.
whyNot.1: 9 accounts only for the Jka-negative frequency (2 / 0.23 = 8.7) and ignores anti-c.
whyNot.3: 10 accounts only for the c-negative frequency (2 / 0.20) and ignores anti-Jka.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Compatibility testing / antibody identification chapters; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

worked.problem: A patient with anti-E and anti-Fya needs 3 units. In the donor population, 30% are E-positive and 66% are Fy(a+). How many units should be screened?
steps: Convert to antigen-negative frequencies: E-negative = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70; Fy(a-) = 1 - 0.66 = 0.34.
Multiply the independent frequencies: 0.70 × 0.34 = 0.238 (23.8% of donors lack both).
Divide units needed by this frequency: 3 / 0.238 = 12.6.
Always round up, because you cannot screen part of a unit and rounding down would give fewer than the needed units on average.

items.stem: An indirect antiglobulin test (tube method) is read as negative. IgG-coated check cells are then added, and after centrifugation no agglutination is seen. The most likely explanation is:
options: The patient has a positive direct antiglobulin test
Inadequate washing left unbound serum globulin that neutralized the AHG reagent
The serum contains no clinically significant antibody, so the negative result is valid
The tubes were overcentrifuged during the antiglobulin phase
items.why: Check cells are IgG-sensitized and should agglutinate if active anti-IgG remains in the tube. **Failure of check cells to react means the AHG was neutralized, inactive, or never added**, most often because poor washing left free serum IgG behind. The negative IAT is therefore invalid and must be repeated.

whyNot.0: The IAT uses reagent red cells, not the patient's cells, so the patient's DAT status does not explain the loss of AHG activity.
whyNot.2: In a true negative test the anti-IgG remains free and would agglutinate the check cells, so a valid negative still shows a positive check-cell reaction.
whyNot.3: Overcentrifugation tends to cause false-positive readings and would not stop check cells from agglutinating.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antiglobulin test chapter; AABB Technical Manual (current ed.)

items.stem: An antibody reacts at the antiglobulin phase with several panel cells, but all reactivity disappears when the same panel cells are pretreated with ficin. Which specificity best fits this pattern?
items.why: Proteolytic enzymes such as ficin and papain destroy the Fya and Fyb antigens (as well as M and N, with S variably affected). **Loss of reactivity after enzyme treatment** points to an antibody against an enzyme-sensitive antigen such as Fya.

whyNot.0: Lewis antigens are enhanced by enzyme treatment, so anti-Lea reactivity would increase.
whyNot.2: Kidd antigens are enhanced by enzymes, so anti-Jka reactions get stronger.
whyNot.3: Rh antigens such as E are enhanced, not destroyed, by enzyme treatment.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antibody detection and identification chapter

items.stem: A D-negative mother delivers a D-positive infant. Her fetal screen (rosette test) is positive, and a Kleihauer–Betke stain shows 28 fetal cells among 2,000 red cells counted. Assuming a maternal blood volume of 5,000 mL, that each 300-µg vial of RhIG protects against 30 mL of fetal whole blood, and using the AABB rounding rule, how many 300-µg vials should be given?
items.why: Fetal cells = 28 / 2,000 = 1.4%. Fetal whole blood = 1.4 × 50 = 70 mL, and 70 / 30 = 2.33 vials. Because the decimal is below .5, round down to 2 and then add one vial, giving **3 vials**.

whyNot.0: 4 rounds 2.33 up before adding a vial; rounding up applies only when the decimal is .5 or more.
whyNot.1: 6 comes from dividing 70 mL of fetal whole blood by 15 mL (4.67, rounded up to 5, plus one vial); 15 mL is the fetal red cell volume one vial covers, so whole blood must be divided by 30 mL.
whyNot.3: 2 rounds 2.33 down but leaves out the extra vial that the AABB rule always adds.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual (current ed.), Perinatal issues in transfusion practice (RhIG dosing); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter

worked.problem: A Kleihauer–Betke stain shows 34 fetal cells per 2,000 red cells in a D-negative mother (maternal blood volume 5,000 mL; 30 mL fetal whole blood per 300-µg vial). How many vials?
steps: Fetal whole blood volume = % fetal cells × 50 = 1.7 × 50 = 85 mL (50 = 5,000 mL / 100).
AABB rule: if the decimal is .5 or more, round up and add one vial; if below .5, round down and add one vial. Here 2.83 rounds up to 3, plus 1 = 4.

items.stem: Two weeks after Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia, a young adult develops hemolytic anemia. The DAT is positive with anti-C3d and negative with anti-IgG, and the cold agglutinin titer is markedly raised. The autoantibody most likely has which specificity?
items.why: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection classically induces a polyclonal IgM cold autoantibody with anti-I specificity. The IgM binds in the cooler peripheral circulation, fixes complement and then detaches, **leaving only C3d on the red cells**.

whyNot.0: Anti-e-like specificities are typical of warm IgG autoantibodies, which would give a positive anti-IgG DAT.
whyNot.1: Anti-P is the biphasic IgG Donath-Landsteiner antibody of paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, which does not produce a high cold agglutinin titer.
whyNot.3: Anti-i cold agglutinins are typically associated with infectious mononucleosis (EBV), not Mycoplasma.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Autoimmune hemolytic anemias chapter

items.stem: Which cell can kill a virus-infected cell that has lost its MHC class I expression, without any prior sensitization?
items.why: NK cells are innate lymphocytes whose inhibitory receptors recognize self MHC class I. When a cell loses class I (the 'missing self'), **inhibition is lifted and the NK cell kills it** using perforin and granzymes, with no prior exposure needed.

whyNot.0: Plasma cells secrete antibody and do not kill target cells directly.
whyNot.1: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses rather than kill infected cells.
whyNot.3: Cytotoxic T cells must recognize peptide presented on MHC class I, so they miss cells that have lost class I, and they need prior priming.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Innate immunity chapter

items.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is produced first in a primary immune response and is the most efficient activator of the classical complement pathway?
items.why: IgM is the first antibody made after first exposure to an antigen. Because it is a pentamer, **a single bound IgM molecule can engage C1q**, making it the most efficient classical-pathway activator.

whyNot.0: IgG dominates the secondary response, and two IgG molecules must bind close together to activate C1.
whyNot.2: IgE binds to mast cells and basophils and does not activate the classical pathway.
whyNot.3: IgA does not activate the classical pathway and is mainly a secretory, mucosal antibody.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Immunoglobulins chapter

items.stem: Digestion of IgG with pepsin produces:
options: One F(ab')2 fragment, with the Fc portion broken into small peptides
Two Fab fragments and one intact Fc fragment
Two separate heavy chains and two separate light chains
A J chain and a secretory component
items.why: Pepsin cleaves below the hinge-region disulfide bonds, so the two antigen-binding arms stay joined as **one divalent F(ab')2 fragment**, while the Fc portion is broken into smaller peptides. Because F(ab')2 keeps both binding sites, it can still crosslink antigen and cause agglutination or precipitation.

whyNot.1: Two Fab fragments plus an intact Fc are the products of papain digestion, which cuts above the hinge disulfide bonds.
whyNot.2: Separated heavy and light chains come from reducing the interchain disulfide bonds (for example with 2-mercaptoethanol), not from pepsin.
whyNot.3: The J chain and secretory component belong to polymeric IgM or IgA, not to monomeric IgG.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Immunoglobulins chapter

items.stem: Which IgG subclass is the most efficient activator of the classical complement pathway and also has the shortest serum half-life?
items.why: IgG3 has a long, flexible hinge region that makes it the best complement activator among the subclasses (IgG3 > IgG1 > IgG2, with IgG4 essentially inactive). **Its half-life is only about 7 days**, compared with about 3 weeks for the other subclasses.

whyNot.1: IgG1 is the most abundant subclass and fixes complement well, but less efficiently than IgG3, and its half-life is about 3 weeks.
whyNot.2: IgG4 does not activate the classical complement pathway.
whyNot.3: IgG2 is a weak complement activator and is associated mainly with responses to polysaccharide antigens.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Immunoglobulins chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: The signature cytokine of Th1 cells, which activates macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens, is:
items.why: Th1 cells are defined by **interferon-gamma** production, which activates macrophages and promotes cell-mediated immunity against intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria. Th1 responses also underlie type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.

whyNot.1: Interleukin-5 is a Th2 cytokine that promotes eosinophil growth and activation.
whyNot.2: Interleukin-17 is produced by Th17 cells and mainly recruits neutrophils.
whyNot.3: Interleukin-4 is the defining Th2 cytokine, driving B-cell class switching to IgE.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Cell-mediated immunity / T-cell chapter

items.stem: Which regulatory protein stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) and prolongs its activity?
items.why: Properdin binds C3bBb and **lengthens the half-life of the convertase several-fold**, making it the only positive regulator in this list. The other proteins limit complement activation.

whyNot.0: Factor I is a serine protease that cleaves and inactivates C3b and C4b with the help of cofactors.
whyNot.2: C1 inhibitor inactivates C1r, C1s and the lectin-pathway MASPs; it does not act on C3bBb.
whyNot.3: Factor H displaces Bb from C3b, speeding decay of the convertase, and acts as a cofactor for factor I.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Complement system chapter

items.stem: In a pretransplant complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) crossmatch, a kidney recipient's serum lyses the prospective donor's T lymphocytes. This result most directly indicates that the recipient has preformed antibodies against donor:
items.why: Resting T lymphocytes express HLA class I but little or no class II, so a positive T-cell CDC crossmatch points to **donor-specific HLA class I antibodies**. These antibodies can cause hyperacute or early antibody-mediated rejection.

whyNot.0: ABO compatibility is established by red cell typing, not by lymphocyte cytotoxicity testing.
whyNot.2: Minor histocompatibility antigens mainly provoke T-cell responses and are not what a CDC antibody crossmatch detects.
whyNot.3: Class II antibodies are detected with donor B cells, which express both classes; they typically give a positive B-cell but negative T-cell crossmatch.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Transplantation immunology chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: A patient treated for secondary syphilis five years ago is now asymptomatic. Current results: RPR nonreactive; TP-PA reactive. The best interpretation is:
options: A biologic false-positive reaction caused by an autoimmune disorder
Prozone in the RPR masking a high antibody level
A serologic pattern expected after successful treatment
items.why: Nontreponemal tests such as the RPR decline and often become nonreactive after effective therapy. **Treponemal tests such as TP-PA usually remain reactive for life**, so this pattern fits past, treated syphilis.

whyNot.0: Biologic false positives typically affect nontreponemal tests (RPR reactive, treponemal test nonreactive), which is the opposite pattern.
whyNot.1: Prozone occurs with very high antibody levels, typically in active secondary syphilis, not in an asymptomatic patient years after treatment.
whyNot.3: Active secondary syphilis gives a reactive RPR, usually at a high titer.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Syphilis chapter

items.stem: Three weeks after streptococcal impetigo, a child develops acute glomerulonephritis. The ASO titer is within the reference range. Which test is most useful for documenting a recent group A streptococcal infection?
items.why: After skin infections the ASO response is often weak, partly because skin lipids inactivate streptolysin O. **Anti-DNase B rises after both skin and throat infections**, so it is the preferred test when post-streptococcal disease follows impetigo.

whyNot.1: The Weil-Felix test detects cross-reacting antibodies in rickettsial infections.
whyNot.2: Cold agglutinin titers are associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, not streptococcal infection.
whyNot.3: The heterophile antibody test is used for infectious mononucleosis (EBV).

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Streptococcal infections chapter

items.stem: A health care worker's hepatitis B panel shows: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, total anti-HBc negative. This pattern indicates:
options: Immunity from a past natural infection
items.why: The hepatitis B vaccine contains only HBsAg, so a vaccinated person makes anti-HBs but **no anti-HBc**. A negative anti-HBc rules out past or current natural infection.

whyNot.1: Immunity after natural infection shows both anti-HBs and anti-HBc.
whyNot.2: Acute infection shows a positive HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc.
whyNot.3: Chronic infection shows HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months with a positive anti-HBc.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Viral hepatitis chapter

items.stem: In the Davidsohn differential absorption test, the heterophile antibodies of infectious mononucleosis are:
options: Absorbed by neither guinea pig kidney cells nor beef red cells
Absorbed by beef red cells but not by guinea pig kidney cells
Absorbed by both guinea pig kidney cells and beef red cells
Absorbed by guinea pig kidney cells but not by beef red cells
items.why: Guinea pig kidney carries the Forssman antigen but not the IM antigen, while beef red cells carry the IM antigen. **IM heterophile antibodies are therefore removed by beef cells but not by guinea pig kidney**, which separates them from Forssman and serum-sickness antibodies.

whyNot.0: IM heterophile antibodies are removed by beef red cells, so a no-absorption pattern does not describe them.
whyNot.2: Absorption by both reagents is the pattern of serum-sickness heterophile antibodies.
whyNot.3: Absorption by guinea pig kidney but not beef cells is the pattern of Forssman antibodies.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Epstein-Barr virus / infectious mononucleosis chapter

items.stem: Which is the most appropriate clinical use of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)?
options: Detecting ovarian cancer in a woman with a pelvic mass
Confirming a diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma
Monitoring for recurrence after surgical removal of a colorectal cancer
Population screening for colorectal cancer in adults
items.why: CEA is neither sensitive nor specific enough for screening; it is raised in smokers and in benign liver, bowel and lung disease. **Its main value is serial monitoring after colorectal cancer resection**, where a rising level suggests recurrence.

whyNot.0: CA 125, not CEA, is the marker used in evaluating ovarian cancer.
whyNot.1: Alpha-fetoprotein, not CEA, is the main serum marker for hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyNot.3: CEA is not recommended for screening because of its poor sensitivity for early cancer and its many benign causes of elevation.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Tumor markers chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: On HEp-2 indirect immunofluorescence, a patient's ANA shows discrete, evenly sized speckles (roughly 40 to 60 per nucleus) in interphase cells, and in mitotic cells the speckles line up with the condensed chromosomes. This pattern is most strongly associated with:
items.why: This is the centromere pattern: the antibodies bind kinetochore proteins, so the speckles follow the chromosomes in dividing cells. **Anticentromere antibodies are most strongly linked to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST)**.

whyNot.0: Drug-induced lupus typically gives a homogeneous pattern due to anti-histone antibodies.
whyNot.1: Sjögren syndrome is classically linked to a fine speckled pattern from anti-SS-A/Ro and anti-SS-B/La.
whyNot.2: SLE is classically linked to homogeneous (anti-dsDNA, anti-nucleosome) or speckled (anti-Sm) patterns.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Autoimmunity (antinuclear antibodies) chapter

items.stem: In a real-time PCR assay running at 100% efficiency, sample A crosses the threshold at cycle 18 and sample B at cycle 24. Compared with sample B, sample A contained:
items.why: A lower threshold cycle (Ct) means more starting template, because fewer doublings are needed to reach the threshold. The 6-cycle difference at 100% efficiency equals 2 to the 6th power, so **sample A had about 64 times more target**.

whyNot.0: This reverses the relationship; a lower Ct means more target, not less.
whyNot.1: Each cycle doubles the product, so 6 cycles is a 64-fold (2 to the 6th) difference, not a 6-fold one.
whyNot.2: This both reverses the direction and treats the cycle difference as linear instead of exponential.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Molecular diagnostic techniques chapter

items.stem: A single control result for a quantitative serologic assay falls above the mean + 3 SD on the Levey-Jennings chart. Under the Westgard multirule system, this 1-3s violation chiefly indicates:
options: An expected event in about 1 of 20 runs; accept the run
Systematic error; accept the run with a warning
A shift that must be confirmed over six more runs before acting
items.why: The 1-3s rule is a rejection rule that is most sensitive to random error (it can also catch large systematic error). **Patient results from the run are held** until the cause is found and corrected.

whyNot.0: About 1 in 20 values is expected beyond 2 SD; a value beyond 3 SD is expected only about 0.3% of the time.
whyNot.1: 1-3s is a rejection rule, not a warning; the warning rule is 1-2s.
whyNot.2: A shift is shown by consecutive values on one side of the mean (such as the 10x rule), not by a single outlier, and a 1-3s violation calls for immediate rejection.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Quality assurance / laboratory safety chapter; Westgard QC multirule system

items.stem: A plugged-in centrifuge starts to smoke and catches fire. Under the standard fire classification, this is a:
items.why: **Class C fires involve energized electrical equipment.** Use a carbon dioxide or dry chemical (ABC) extinguisher, cut the power if it is safe to do so, and never use water.

whyNot.0: Class D fires involve combustible metals such as magnesium or sodium.
whyNot.1: Class A fires involve ordinary combustibles such as paper, wood and cloth.
whyNot.2: Class B fires involve flammable liquids and gases such as solvents.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology: A Laboratory Perspective, 5th ed., Laboratory safety chapter; NFPA fire classification (also used in the Philippine Fire Code)

items.stem: A healthy donor's red cells react 4+ with anti-A, do not react with anti-B, and do not agglutinate with Dolichos biflorus lectin. Her plasma agglutinates B cells 4+ and A1 cells 1+ at room temperature, but does not react with A2 cells, group O cells, or her own cells. The most likely explanation is that she is:
options: Group A1 with a cold-reactive autoantibody
Group A2 with anti-A1 in her plasma
Group A3 with anti-A1 in her plasma
Group Ax with anti-A1 in her plasma
items.why: Strong anti-A reactivity with no reaction to Dolichos biflorus (the anti-A1 lectin) identifies **group A2** red cells. A minority of A2 (and a larger share of A2B) people form anti-A1, which agglutinates A1 cells but spares A2 cells; the negative group O cells and autocontrol exclude an alloantibody to another antigen or an autoantibody.

whyNot.0: A cold autoantibody would also react with her own cells and with group O cells, and an A1 person's cells would agglutinate with Dolichos biflorus.
whyNot.2: A3 cells give a characteristic mixed-field reaction with anti-A, not a strong 4+ reaction.
whyNot.3: Ax cells react weakly or not at all with anti-A (they react better with anti-A,B), so a 4+ anti-A reaction argues against Ax.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., ABO blood group system chapter (ABO subgroups); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A donor's red cells react with anti-D, anti-C, and anti-e, but not with anti-c or anti-E. Using Wiener shorthand, the most probable Rh genotype is:
items.why: The cells are D+, C+, c−, E−, e+, so both haplotypes must carry C and e; with D present the commonest haplotype is DCe (R1), giving **R1R1** (DCe/DCe). DCe/dCe (R1r') is also possible, but because no anti-d exists and r' is rare, R1R1 is the most probable genotype.

whyNot.0: R1r (DCe/dce) carries c on the r haplotype, so the cells would react with anti-c.
whyNot.1: R1R2 (DCe/DcE) carries both c and E on the R2 haplotype, so the cells would react with anti-c and anti-E.
whyNot.2: R2R2 (DcE/DcE) would be C-negative and E-positive, the opposite of these results.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter (Fisher-Race and Wiener nomenclature)

items.stem: A woman has a mild, compensated hemolytic anemia with stomatocytes on her blood smear. Her red cells give no reaction with anti-D, anti-C, anti-c, anti-E, anti-e, or anti-LW. The most likely phenotype is:
items.why: Absence of all Rh antigens together with LW defines the **Rh-null** phenotype, caused by either a regulator (RHAG) mutation or an amorph RHD/RHCE background. Because the Rh protein complex helps maintain membrane structure, Rh-null cells are stomatocytic and have a shortened survival, producing a compensated hemolytic anemia.

whyNot.1: D-deletion cells lack C, c, E, and e but still express D, often strongly, so they would react with anti-D.
whyNot.2: Ordinary D-negative (rr) cells express c and e, so they would react with anti-c and anti-e.
whyNot.3: The McLeod phenotype is a Kell-system defect (absent Kx with weak Kell antigens) with acanthocytes, not loss of Rh antigens.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Rh blood group system chapter (Rh-null syndrome); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: Red cells of the Fy(a−b−) phenotype, which is common among people of West African ancestry, resist invasion by which malaria parasite?
items.why: The Duffy glycoprotein (DARC/ACKR1) is the receptor that **Plasmodium vivax** uses to invade red cells. People with the Fy(a−b−) phenotype (usually from a GATA-box promoter mutation that silences Duffy expression only in the erythroid line) are therefore largely resistant to vivax malaria.

whyNot.0: P. falciparum invades red cells mainly through glycophorins and other receptors, so Duffy-null cells are not protected from it.
whyNot.1: P. malariae does not depend on the Duffy glycoprotein, and Duffy-null people are not protected from it.
whyNot.3: P. ovale is in fact common in West Africa, where the Duffy-null phenotype predominates, so Duffy-null cells do not block it.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other blood group systems chapter (Duffy); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: In a donor population, 9% of people type K-positive. K and k are codominant alleles of the Kell system; treat them as the only two alleles and assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the frequency of the K allele?
items.why: Start from the antigen-negative phenotype, because only kk people are K-negative: q² = 1 − 0.09 = 0.91, so q (k) = √0.91 = 0.954. Then p (K) = 1 − 0.954 = **0.046**. Most K-positive people are therefore heterozygous (2pq ≈ 0.088), and KK homozygotes are only about 0.2% of the population.

whyNot.1: 0.09 is the K-positive phenotype frequency, which includes both KK and Kk people; it is not the allele frequency.
whyNot.2: 0.30 is the square root of 0.09, which wrongly assumes all K-positive people are homozygous (KK = p²).
whyNot.3: 0.954 is the frequency of the k allele (the square root of 0.91), not of the K allele.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Basic genetics chapter (Hardy-Weinberg principle and population genetics)

worked.problem: In a population, 84% of people are positive for antigen X, which is controlled by two codominant alleles (X and x). Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, find the frequency of allele X and the percentage of people who are homozygous XX.
steps: Antigen-negative people (xx) make up 1 − 0.84 = 0.16 of the population, and this equals q².
Homozygous XX = p² = 0.60² = 0.36; heterozygous Xx = 2pq = 2 × 0.60 × 0.40 = 0.48. Check: 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, matching the antigen-positive frequency.
worked.result: Allele X frequency = 0.60; 36% of the population is homozygous XX.

items.stem: The Di(a) antigen is a useful anthropologic marker because it is found mainly in people of East Asian and Native American ancestry and is rare in people of European or African ancestry. On which red cell membrane protein are the Diego system antigens carried?
items.why: The Diego antigens, including Dia/Dib and Wra/Wrb, sit on **band 3**, the red cell anion exchanger (AE1, SLC4A1). Anti-Dia, though uncommon, can cause hemolytic transfusion reactions and HDFN, which is why it matters in Asian and Native American populations.

whyNot.0: Glycophorin A carries the M and N antigens of the MNS system.
whyNot.1: Glycophorin C (and its variant glycophorin D) carries the Gerbich system antigens.
whyNot.2: The Duffy glycoprotein carries the Fya and Fyb antigens and is the chemokine receptor used by P. vivax.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other blood group systems chapter (Diego); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., blood group antigens and antibodies chapter

items.stem: Most whole blood collection sets now include a diversion pouch that captures the first few tens of milliliters of blood drawn from the donor. The main purpose of this pouch is to:
options: Remove leukocytes that cause febrile reactions
Reduce bacterial contamination of the unit from skin
Lower the citrate content of the collected unit
Clear air from the tubing to prevent embolism
items.why: The first blood drawn can carry a core of skin (the skin plug) and resident bacteria such as coagulase-negative staphylococci that survive arm disinfection. Diverting it away from the main bag **reduces bacterial contamination of the unit from skin**, which matters most for platelets stored at room temperature.

whyNot.0: Leukocytes are removed by leukoreduction filters; diverting the first small volume does not meaningfully lower the white cell content of the unit.
whyNot.2: The anticoagulant volume is fixed in the primary bag; the diverted blood does not change the citrate-to-blood ratio of the unit.
whyNot.3: Air embolism is prevented by proper tubing and clamp handling, not by the diversion pouch.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., whole blood collection chapter; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., donor selection and collection chapter

items.stem: During a plateletpheresis donation using ACD-A anticoagulant, the donor reports tingling around the lips and in the fingertips. Her pulse and blood pressure are stable. The most likely cause and an appropriate first response are:
options: Vasovagal reaction; stop the procedure and raise the donor's legs
Air embolism; turn the donor onto the left side with head down
Citrate toxicity; slow the return rate and give oral calcium
Ethylene oxide allergy; give an antihistamine and continue
items.why: Citrate returned to the donor binds ionized calcium, and the resulting **hypocalcemia** first appears as perioral and fingertip tingling. It is managed by slowing the return (citrate infusion) rate and, per facility protocol, giving oral calcium; untreated it can progress to muscle cramps, tetany, or arrhythmia.

whyNot.0: A vasovagal reaction presents with pallor, sweating, lightheadedness, and often a slow pulse and low blood pressure, not isolated perioral tingling.
whyNot.1: Air embolism presents with sudden cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or cyanosis, not tingling around the mouth.
whyNot.3: An allergy to ethylene oxide used to sterilize kits causes urticaria, flushing, or anaphylaxis rather than paresthesias.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., apheresis chapter (donor adverse reactions); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., apheresis chapter

items.stem: Which set of changes develops in red cells during refrigerated storage at 1–6 °C (the red cell storage lesion)?
options: Decreased 2,3-DPG, increased plasma potassium, decreased pH
Increased 2,3-DPG, decreased plasma potassium, increased pH
Decreased 2,3-DPG, decreased plasma potassium, increased ATP
Increased ATP, increased pH, decreased plasma hemoglobin
items.why: Continued glycolysis produces lactate, so pH falls and **2,3-DPG drops** (which raises hemoglobin's oxygen affinity), while the cold-inhibited Na+/K+ pump lets potassium leak into the plasma. ATP gradually declines and plasma hemoglobin rises; 2,3-DPG is regenerated within hours to days after transfusion.

whyNot.1: Every change is reversed: 2,3-DPG falls as the pH drops, and potassium leaks out of cells because the cold slows the Na+/K+ pump.
whyNot.2: Plasma potassium rises rather than falls, and ATP falls gradually during storage.
whyNot.3: ATP and pH fall as glycolysis produces lactate, and plasma hemoglobin rises as some cells hemolyze.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Preservation and storage of blood chapter (storage lesion); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: Under AABB standards, platelets (whole blood-derived or apheresis) intended for conventional storage are kept at:
items.why: Conventional platelets are stored at **20–24 °C with continuous gentle agitation**, which keeps them functional and in circulation after transfusion and maintains gas exchange to prevent a fall in pH. The trade-off of room-temperature storage is a higher risk of bacterial growth, which is why the shelf life is short and bacterial risk control is required.

whyNot.0: Refrigeration activates platelets and causes rapid clearance after transfusion, so conventional platelets are not refrigerated.
whyNot.1: Without agitation, gas exchange through the bag is poor, lactate builds up, and the pH falls; agitation may be interrupted only for a limited time (no more than 24 hours), such as during shipping.
whyNot.2: These are the conditions for red cells; cold-stored platelets kept this way are a separate, special-indication product, not conventional storage.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., component storage chapter; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Preservation and storage of blood chapter

items.stem: When platelets are prepared from whole blood by the platelet-rich plasma (PRP) method, the correct centrifugation sequence is:
options: A heavy spin of whole blood, then a light spin of the PRP
A light spin of whole blood, then a heavy spin of the PRP
Two heavy spins, the second performed on the PRP
Two light spins, the second performed on the PRP
items.why: A **light (soft) spin first** leaves platelets suspended in the plasma above the red cells; this PRP is expressed into a satellite bag. A heavy (hard) spin of the PRP then pellets the platelets, most of the plasma is removed, and the platelets are rested before being resuspended in the remaining plasma.

whyNot.0: A heavy first spin would pack platelets with the red cells and buffy coat, so little would be left in the plasma to harvest.
whyNot.2: The first spin must be light; a heavy first spin sediments most platelets along with the cells.
whyNot.3: A light second spin would leave most platelets suspended in the plasma instead of forming a pellet.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Component preparation chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., blood component preparation chapter

items.stem: An adult with a body surface area (BSA) of 1.8 m² receives an apheresis platelet unit containing 3.6 × 10¹¹ platelets. The platelet count is 8 × 10³/µL before and 33 × 10³/µL 1 hour after transfusion. What is the corrected count increment (CCI)?
items.why: CCI = (post-count − pre-count, per µL) × BSA (m²) ÷ platelets transfused (× 10¹¹). Here (33,000 − 8,000) × 1.8 ÷ 3.6 = **12,500**. A 1-hour CCI well above 7,500 indicates an adequate response, which argues against immune refractoriness.

whyNot.0: 6,944 comes from omitting the BSA: 25,000 ÷ 3.6. The CCI corrects for patient size by multiplying by BSA.
whyNot.1: 16,500 uses the post-transfusion count (33,000) instead of the increment (33,000 − 8,000).
whyNot.3: 3,858 comes from dividing by the BSA instead of multiplying by it: 25,000 ÷ (1.8 × 3.6).

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Component therapy chapter (platelet transfusion and refractoriness); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

worked.problem: A patient with a BSA of 1.6 m² receives a pool of whole blood-derived platelets estimated to contain 3.3 × 10¹¹ platelets. The count rises from 5 × 10³/µL to 20 × 10³/µL at 1 hour. Calculate the CCI and judge the response, using 7,500 as the cutoff for an adequate 1-hour CCI.
steps: Divide by the number of platelets transfused in units of 10¹¹: 24,000 ÷ 3.3 = 7,273.
Compare with the cutoff: 7,273 is below 7,500, so the response is poor; if repeated after another fresh, ABO-compatible transfusion, evaluate for refractoriness (for example, HLA antibodies).

items.stem: Within minutes of starting a plasma transfusion, an afebrile patient develops hypotension, bronchospasm, and generalized urticaria. Workup shows undetectable serum IgA and the presence of anti-IgA. For future transfusions, the best choice is:
options: IgA-deficient donor components or washed cells
Leukoreduced components given with an antihistamine
Irradiated components from any compatible donor
Standard components given with an antipyretic
items.why: Anaphylaxis without fever in a patient with absent IgA and anti-IgA points to an antibody against **donor plasma IgA**. Prevention requires removing the antigen: plasma and platelets from IgA-deficient donors, and red cells or platelets washed to remove residual plasma.

whyNot.1: Leukoreduction lowers the risk of febrile reactions and HLA alloimmunization but leaves the IgA-containing plasma in place.
whyNot.2: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes to prevent TA-GVHD; it does not remove IgA.
whyNot.3: An antipyretic treats febrile reactions and does nothing to prevent IgA-mediated anaphylaxis.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Adverse effects of blood transfusion chapter (anaphylactic reactions); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: A red cell unit stored for several weeks at 1–6 °C causes septic shock and endotoxemia in the recipient. Which organism is classically implicated, because it is a gram-negative rod that grows at refrigerator temperature and uses iron?
items.why: **Yersinia enterocolitica** is psychrophilic (it grows at 1–6 °C), uses iron released from stored red cells, and produces endotoxin, so older red cell units are the classic source. It may come from a donor with mild, unrecognized gastrointestinal infection.

whyNot.0: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are the commonest contaminants of room-temperature platelets, but they are gram-positive and grow poorly in refrigerated red cells.
whyNot.1: T. pallidum survives poorly at refrigerator temperature, so transmission is linked to fresh components, and it does not cause endotoxic shock.
whyNot.2: Bacillus species are gram-positive spore formers usually linked to platelet contamination, not to cold-stored red cells.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Transfusion-transmitted diseases chapter (bacterial contamination); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: When a patient's antibody screen is negative and there is no history of clinically significant antibodies, an immediate-spin crossmatch is mainly intended to detect:
options: IgG alloantibodies such as anti-K or anti-Fya
ABO incompatibility between donor and recipient
Incompatibility due to D type in D-negative recipients
Donor red cells already coated with IgG
items.why: With a negative screen and no antibody history, the immediate-spin (room-temperature, no incubation) crossmatch serves as a final check for **ABO incompatibility**, catching errors in labeling, typing, or unit selection. Its main limitation is missing IgG antibodies to antigens absent from the screening cells.

whyNot.0: IgG alloantibodies usually need 37 °C incubation and antiglobulin reagent, which the immediate-spin crossmatch omits.
whyNot.2: D typing of donors and patients prevents this; anti-D is IgG and is not reliably detected at immediate spin.
whyNot.3: A positive donor DAT is shown by an antiglobulin test, not by an immediate-spin crossmatch.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion testing chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., pretransfusion testing chapter

items.stem: A patient's 3-cell antibody screen and autologous control are negative. One of four ABO-compatible red cell units is 2+ incompatible at the antiglobulin phase; the other three are compatible. The DAT on the incompatible donor unit is negative, and an 11-cell panel that includes cells homozygous for Kidd, Duffy, and MNS antigens is also nonreactive. The most likely explanation is that the patient has:
options: A warm IgG autoantibody to red cells
An alloantibody to a high-prevalence antigen
An antibody to a low-prevalence donor antigen
items.why: Reactivity with only one donor unit, while screening cells, panel cells (including homozygous cells that rule out a dosage-related miss), and the autologous control are all negative and the donor DAT is negative, points to **an antibody to a low-prevalence antigen** carried by that donor. Such antigens are absent from most reagent cells, so the antibody is found only by the crossmatch; the unit is simply not used.

whyNot.0: A warm autoantibody would make the autologous control and all screening and panel cells react.
whyNot.1: An antibody to a high-prevalence antigen would react with nearly all screening and panel cells, not with just one donor unit.
whyNot.3: Rouleaux affect all cells tested in the patient's plasma and are washed away before the antiglobulin phase, so they would not affect one unit only.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Pretransfusion testing and antibody identification chapters; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: Which situation calls for a direct antiglobulin test (DAT) rather than an indirect antiglobulin test?
options: Investigating suspected HDFN using the newborn's red cells
Screening a patient's plasma for unexpected antibodies
Testing a donor's red cells for weak D
Performing an antiglobulin crossmatch with donor cells
items.why: The DAT detects antibody or complement that has **coated red cells in vivo**, as in HDFN, hemolytic transfusion reactions, and autoimmune or drug-induced hemolysis. The IAT detects in vitro sensitization, so it is used for antibody screening and identification, crossmatching, weak D testing, and red cell antigen typing.

whyNot.1: Antibody screening detects free antibody in plasma by incubating it with reagent cells, which is an indirect antiglobulin test.
whyNot.2: Weak D testing incubates the cells with anti-D in vitro before adding AHG, so it is an indirect antiglobulin test.
whyNot.3: The crossmatch incubates recipient plasma with donor cells in vitro, which is an indirect antiglobulin test.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antihuman globulin test chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: An antibody that reacts best at room temperature appears to be anti-P1. Which substance can be used in a neutralization test to help confirm this specificity?
items.why: P1 substance occurs in **hydatid cyst fluid** (Echinococcus) and in pigeon egg white, and these preparations inhibit anti-P1. Loss of reactivity after neutralization, with a dilution control that stays reactive, supports anti-P1 and can expose other antibodies hidden by it.

whyNot.0: Secretor saliva contains soluble ABH (and Lewis) substances and is used to neutralize those antibodies or to determine secretor status, not anti-P1.
whyNot.1: Pooled plasma supplies soluble Chido/Rodgers (C4) substance and is used to neutralize anti-Ch and anti-Rg.
whyNot.2: Human milk contains soluble I substance and can be used to neutralize anti-I, not anti-P1.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Other blood group systems chapter (P system); AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., antibody identification chapter (neutralization)

items.stem: Because of dosage, which antibody should be excluded only with a nonreactive panel cell that is homozygous for the corresponding antigen?
items.why: Antibodies in the MNS, Rh (C, c, E, e), Duffy, and Kidd systems often show dosage, reacting more strongly with cells from homozygotes. **Anti-M** in particular may react with M+N− cells yet miss M+N+ cells, so it should be excluded with a nonreactive M+N− cell.

whyNot.0: Lewis antigens are adsorbed from plasma rather than encoded by codominant alleles on the red cell, so homozygous cells are not used to exclude anti-Lea.
whyNot.2: P1 strength varies widely between individuals, but this is not dosage from codominant alleles, so homozygous cells are not the exclusion rule for anti-P1.
whyNot.3: Exclusion of anti-K is usually accepted with a K+k+ cell because K+k− cells are rare and Kell dosage effects are slight.

items.ref: AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed., antibody identification chapter (exclusion and dosage); Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Antibody identification chapter

items.stem: Which antibody found during a pregnant woman's prenatal antibody screen is least likely to cause HDFN?
items.why: **Lewis antibodies** are mostly IgM, so they do not cross the placenta, and Lewis antigens are poorly developed on fetal and newborn red cells. Lewis antibodies are also common in pregnancy, partly because many women transiently type Le(a−b−) while pregnant.

whyNot.0: Anti-K is IgG and can cause severe HDFN; it also suppresses fetal erythropoiesis, so the anemia can be worse than bilirubin levels suggest.
whyNot.1: Anti-c is IgG and is one of the most important causes of severe HDFN after anti-D.
whyNot.3: Anti-Fya is usually IgG and can cause HDFN, usually mild but occasionally severe.

items.ref: Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn chapter and Lewis system chapter; AABB Technical Manual, 21st ed.

items.stem: C-reactive protein, an acute-phase reactant that binds the phosphocholine of pneumococcal C-polysaccharide, is synthesized mainly by:
options: Plasma cells, in response to bacterial antigens
items.why: CRP is made by **hepatocytes**, mainly under the control of IL-6 (with help from IL-1 and TNF-α). It rises within hours of inflammation or tissue injury, binds phosphocholine in a calcium-dependent way, and activates the classical complement pathway and opsonizes microbes.

whyNot.1: CRP is not an antibody; plasma cells secrete immunoglobulins, whereas CRP is an innate pattern-recognition protein made by the liver.
whyNot.2: Macrophages produce IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α, which drive CRP synthesis, but they do not make CRP themselves.
whyNot.3: IL-8 is a neutrophil chemokine; neutrophils do not synthesize CRP.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., innate immunity / acute-phase reactants chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: Which complement split product is the most potent anaphylatoxin and also a strong chemoattractant for neutrophils?
items.why: The anaphylatoxins C3a, C4a, and C5a cause mast cell degranulation, smooth muscle contraction, and increased vascular permeability, with **C5a** the most potent. C5a is also a powerful chemotactic factor that draws neutrophils and monocytes to the site of complement activation.

whyNot.0: C3b is the major opsonin and part of the C5 convertases; it is not an anaphylatoxin.
whyNot.1: C4a is a weak anaphylatoxin with little chemotactic activity.
whyNot.2: C5b is the larger fragment of C5 and starts assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9); it is not released as an anaphylatoxin.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., complement system chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: A low-molecular-weight drug such as penicillin cannot stimulate antibody production by itself, but it can after binding to a host protein. Such a molecule is called a(n):
items.why: A **hapten** is antigenic (it can bind antibody) but not immunogenic on its own; it becomes immunogenic only when coupled to a larger carrier protein. Penicillin binding to red cell membrane proteins is the classic example, and it is the basis of drug-adsorption immune hemolysis.

whyNot.0: An adjuvant is a substance given with an antigen to enhance the immune response; it is not the small molecule the antibody recognizes.
whyNot.1: The carrier is the larger protein the small molecule binds to, which supplies the T-cell help.
whyNot.3: A mitogen stimulates lymphocytes to divide regardless of their antigen specificity.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., antigens and immunogens chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: Secretory IgA in saliva, tears, and breast milk is a dimer joined by a J chain. What additional feature distinguishes it from most serum IgA?
options: A secretory component from the poly-Ig receptor
A pentameric structure with ten binding sites
An extra constant domain (CH4) on each heavy chain
High-affinity binding to mast cell Fc receptors
items.why: Dimeric IgA made by plasma cells beneath mucosal epithelium binds the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor and is carried across the epithelial cell. At the luminal surface the receptor is cleaved, leaving a fragment attached as the **secretory component**, which protects secretory IgA from proteolysis in mucosal secretions.

whyNot.1: A pentamer with ten antigen-binding sites describes IgM, not secretory IgA.
whyNot.2: IgM and IgE heavy chains have four constant domains; IgA has three plus a hinge region.
whyNot.3: High-affinity binding to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils is a property of IgE.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., immunoglobulin structure and function chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: Peptides from extracellular proteins that a dendritic cell has engulfed and processed in endocytic vesicles are presented on:
options: MHC class I molecules, to CD8+ T cells
MHC class II molecules, to CD4+ T cells
MHC class I molecules, to CD4+ T cells
MHC class II molecules, to CD8+ T cells
items.why: Exogenous antigens are degraded in endosomes and lysosomes, where their peptides are loaded onto **MHC class II** molecules for recognition by CD4+ helper T cells. Endogenous peptides are loaded onto MHC class I for CD8+ T cells; cross-presentation by dendritic cells is a specialized exception.

whyNot.0: MHC class I presents peptides from proteins made inside the cell (endogenous, such as viral proteins) to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
whyNot.2: CD4 binds MHC class II, not class I, so CD4+ T cells are restricted to class II.
whyNot.3: CD8 binds MHC class I, not class II, so CD8+ T cells are restricted to class I.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., cell-mediated immunity / MHC chapter; Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: In a person previously sensitized to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an intradermal tuberculin injection produces induration that peaks at 48–72 hours. This reaction is mediated mainly by:
options: Allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells
IgG antibodies bound to antigens on host cells
Sensitized Th1 cells that activate macrophages
items.why: The tuberculin reaction is the classic type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. Memory **Th1 cells** recognize the antigen, release IFN-γ and other cytokines, and recruit and activate macrophages; this cellular influx takes 48–72 hours, and no antibody is involved.

whyNot.0: IgE-mediated (type I) reactions begin within minutes and cause a wheal and flare, not induration that peaks at 2–3 days.
whyNot.1: Immune-complex (type III) reactions such as the Arthus reaction peak within hours and involve neutrophils, not a 48–72 hour T-cell infiltrate.
whyNot.2: Antibody against cell-surface antigens is type II hypersensitivity, which causes cell lysis or dysfunction, not delayed induration.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., hypersensitivity chapter (type IV); Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine

items.stem: HLA genes lie close together on chromosome 6 and are usually inherited as haplotypes. Ignoring recombination, what is the chance that a patient's full sibling is HLA-identical (shares both haplotypes)?
items.why: Each child gets one of two haplotypes from each parent, giving four equally likely combinations. A given sibling therefore has a **25%** chance of being HLA-identical, 50% of being haploidentical, and 25% of sharing no haplotype, which is why siblings are searched first for a matched stem cell donor.

whyNot.0: 50% is the chance that a sibling shares exactly one haplotype (haploidentical).
whyNot.1: 75% is the chance that a sibling shares at least one haplotype (identical plus haploidentical).
whyNot.3: Only identical twins are certain to be HLA-identical; ordinary siblings each receive a random haplotype from each parent.

items.ref: Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed., transplantation immunology chapter; Harmening, Modern Blood Banking & Transfusion Practices, 7th ed., HLA system chapter

items.stem: The Weil-Felix test, a febrile agglutinin test once used to support a diagnosis of rickettsial infection, uses which antigens?
options: Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK
Sheep or horse red blood cells
items.why: Antibodies made during many rickettsial infections cross-react with somatic antigens of certain **Proteus strains** (P. vulgaris OX19 and OX2, P. mirabilis OXK). The test is cheap but neither sensitive nor specific, so indirect immunofluorescence and molecular methods have largely replaced it.

whyNot.0: Salmonella O and H antigens are used in the Widal test for typhoid fever.
whyNot.2: Killed Brucella cells are used in the Brucella agglutination test for brucellosis.
whyNot.3: Sheep or horse red cells detect the heterophile antibodies of infectious mononucleosis.

items.ref: Turgeon, Immunology & Serology in Laboratory Medicine, rickettsial infections / febrile agglutinins; Stevens, Clinical Immunology & Serology, 5th ed.

items.stem: A patient recovering from acute hepatitis has these results: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, IgM anti-HBc positive. The best interpretation is:
options: Past HBV infection with recovery and immunity
Acute HBV infection in the core window period
items.why: After HBsAg clears and before anti-HBs is detectable, **IgM anti-HBc** may be the only marker of acute infection. This core window is why total or IgM anti-HBc testing is needed to avoid missing recent HBV infection.

whyNot.0: Vaccination produces anti-HBs only; anti-HBc would be negative because the vaccine contains no core antigen.
whyNot.1: Recovery with immunity shows anti-HBs together with IgG (total) anti-HBc, not an isolated IgM anti-HBc.
whyNot.2: Chronic infection is defined by HBsAg persisting for more than 6 months, and HBsAg is negative here.

items.stem: In an indirect ELISA for antibodies to HIV, patient serum is added to wells coated with HIV antigens, incubated, and washed. Which reagent is added next?
items.why: In an indirect ELISA, patient antibody bound to the solid-phase antigen is detected with an **enzyme-labeled anti-human immunoglobulin** conjugate. After another wash, substrate is added, and the color produced is proportional to the antibody bound. Indirect immunofluorescence follows the same logic but uses a fluorochrome-labeled antiglobulin read under a fluorescence microscope.

whyNot.1: The substrate is added only after the enzyme conjugate has bound and unbound conjugate has been washed away.
whyNot.2: A labeled antigen is the second reagent in a double-antigen (sandwich) format, not in an indirect ELISA.
whyNot.3: A labeled anti-HIV antibody is used in competitive or antigen-capture formats, not in an indirect ELISA.

items.stem: Latex agglutination and lateral flow tests on CSF or serum for cryptococcal meningitis detect:
options: Galactomannan from the fungal cell wall
items.why: Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) tests detect the **capsular polysaccharide glucuronoxylomannan** shed into CSF and serum, and they are more sensitive than the India ink preparation. In latex tests, rheumatoid factor can cause false positives, so specimens are pretreated with pronase or tested with controls.

whyNot.0: Antibody tests are insensitive in cryptococcosis; current tests detect circulating antigen rather than the host antibody response.
whyNot.2: Galactomannan antigen testing is used mainly for invasive aspergillosis.
whyNot.3: Beta-D-glucan is a broad fungal marker, but it is typically low or undetectable in cryptococcosis, so it is not the cryptococcal test.

items.stem: A woman at 10 weeks' gestation has positive Toxoplasma gondii IgG and IgM. Her Toxoplasma IgG avidity is high. The best interpretation is that the infection:
options: Was acquired within the past few weeks
Is proven acute because IgM is present
Was acquired months earlier, most likely before conception
Is a false-positive finding in an uninfected woman
items.why: IgG avidity rises over months as affinity maturation proceeds, so **high avidity** excludes infection within the time window set by the assay (several months). Early in pregnancy, this places the infection before conception, which means a very low risk of congenital toxoplasmosis.

whyNot.0: Recent primary infection gives low-avidity IgG, because high-avidity antibody takes months to develop.
whyNot.1: Toxoplasma IgM can persist for many months to years, so a positive IgM alone does not prove recent infection.
whyNot.3: High-avidity IgG indicates true, longstanding infection, not a false-positive reaction in an uninfected person.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a testicular mass. His serum AFP is markedly elevated and his hCG is mildly elevated. These findings indicate:
options: A pure classic seminoma of the testis
A Leydig cell tumor of the testis
items.why: AFP is produced by yolk sac (endodermal sinus) elements and, to a lesser degree, embryonal carcinoma, so **an elevated AFP signals a nonseminomatous component** even if the biopsy suggests seminoma. AFP, hCG, and LDH are used together for diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of testicular germ cell tumors.

whyNot.0: Pure seminomas may raise hCG mildly but do not produce AFP; a raised AFP rules out a pure seminoma.
whyNot.2: Leydig cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that may secrete androgens or estrogens but not AFP.
whyNot.3: Testicular lymphoma, seen mostly in older men, does not produce AFP or hCG.

items.stem: Which condition is an example of type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity?
items.why: In **serum sickness**, antibodies to a foreign protein form soluble immune complexes that deposit in vessels, joints, and glomeruli, activate complement, and attract neutrophils. Other type III examples include the Arthus reaction, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and the nephritis of SLE.

whyNot.0: Antibody binding to antigens on transfused red cells is type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity.
whyNot.1: Contact dermatitis is type IV (T-cell-mediated, delayed) hypersensitivity.
whyNot.2: Hay fever is type I (IgE-mediated, immediate) hypersensitivity.

items.stem: Which technique detects specific RNA molecules that have been separated by gel electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and hybridized with a labeled probe?
items.why: Blot names follow the target: Southern for DNA, **Northern for RNA**, and Western for protein. In a Northern blot, RNA is separated under denaturing conditions, transferred to a membrane, and detected with a labeled complementary probe, which shows both the presence and the size of a transcript.

whyNot.1: A Southern blot detects DNA fragments, usually after restriction enzyme digestion, using a labeled nucleic acid probe.
whyNot.2: A Western blot detects proteins separated by electrophoresis, using labeled antibodies rather than nucleic acid probes.
whyNot.3: FISH hybridizes fluorescent probes to DNA or RNA within intact cells or chromosomes, with no electrophoretic separation.

items.stem: Most fatal acute hemolytic transfusion reactions caused by ABO-incompatible blood result from:
options: Failure of the AHG crossmatch to detect weak IgG antibodies
Errors in identifying the patient, sample, or unit
Undetected weak D expression in the recipient
items.why: Most ABO-incompatible transfusions trace back to **identification errors**: a wrong blood in tube sample, mislabeling, or transfusing a unit to the wrong patient at the bedside. Quality assurance therefore stresses positive patient identification at sample collection and at the bedside, label checks, and (where used) a second-sample confirmation of ABO group.

whyNot.0: ABO antibodies are mainly IgM and react strongly at room temperature, so ABO incompatibility is not missed by antiglobulin technique.
whyNot.1: Licensed ABO reagents are potent and controlled daily, so reagent failure is rarely the cause.
whyNot.3: Weak D affects Rh typing and anti-D, not ABO incompatibility.
